I picked **candidate 4**. This is a rough estimate worked out in my head, not a simulation. Candidate 1 is out because it has only 28 pairs instead of 30.

**Losses common to every plan.** The first orders only arrive on day 2. On day 1 both products run short (about 21 units of product 0 and about 21 of product 1), so every plan pays the same penalty there. Orders placed on days 28–29 would arrive after day 29; candidate 0 (and candidate 2) don't place them, so nothing is lost on that either.

**How the plans differ: order size compared with the forecast.** Each plan orders the forecast for two days ahead times some factor. Average real demand is about 1.046 × the forecast.
- **Candidate 3 (×1.0)** orders slightly less than average demand, so stock drifts down and shortages build. A missed unit of product 0 costs 17 (9 lost margin plus 8 penalty); for product 1 it costs 7. Daily demand varies by about ±30%, and with no reserve stock the shortages cost a lot.
- **Candidate 0 (×1.25)** builds up surplus of product 0 at about 7 units a day. Product 0 only lasts 5 days, so the extra gets written off at 10 per unit, and holding the large stock costs about 100 a day.
- **Candidate 7** orders product 0 at about ×1.2, which is too much, and product 1 at ×1.0, which is too little.
- **Candidate 5** orders ×1.15 for the first half, then switches to ×1.0. Demand rises in the second half, so the reserve it built up runs out.
- **Candidate 6 (×1.05)** barely covers average demand and leaves little reserve against swings.
- **Candidate 4 (×1.1 for both products)** builds reserve slowly, about 2 units a day for product 0. That reserve absorbs demand swings before it gets old enough to spoil, and with the oldest stock sold first, little is written off. Its stock stays far below the 256-unit limit.

**Candidate 2 (order every other day, ×1.07).** It saves about 15 × 30 = 450 in daily order fees. But keeping each batch an extra night costs about 37 per two-day cycle, roughly the same 30 it saves per cycle. Its large deliveries, such as 208 units after day 20, could also come close to the warehouse limit. With a slightly smaller factor, it comes out no better than candidate 4.

**Robustness to random demand.** Candidate 4 handles demand above the forecast better than the ×1.0–1.05 plans. When demand is below the forecast, it loses less to write-offs than the ×1.2–1.25 plans.

**Выбор: кандидат 4.** Это оценка по прикидке в уме, точной симуляции я не делал. Разница между 4, 6 и 7 небольшая и может зависеть от конкретных реализаций спроса.

**Отсев**
- **Кандидат 1** не проходит: в плане 28 пар вместо обязательных 30.
- **Кандидат 2** заказывает раз в два дня и экономит около 14 × 30 = 420 на фиксированной плате. Но каждая партия лишнюю ночь лежит на складе: примерно 35 × 0,6 + 45 × 0,4 ≈ 39 на каждую пару дней, то есть около 550 за период. Это больше экономии. Кроме того, крупные приходы (например, 72 + 136 в заказе дня 20 плюс остатки) могут упереться в лимит 256, и излишек пропадёт.

**Ежедневные планы.** Все они заказывают в день t прогноз спроса на день t + 2, умноженный на разный коэффициент:
- кандидат 3 — ×1,0;
- кандидат 6 — ×1,05;
- кандидат 4 — ×1,1;
- кандидат 0 — ×1,2 по обоим товарам;
- кандидат 7 — ×1,2 по товару 0 и ×1,0 по товару 1;
- кандидат 5 — ×1,15 в первой половине, потом ×1,0.

Средний спрос — 1,046 × прогноз. Нехватка в первые два дня (приходов ещё нет) одинакова у всех и на сравнение не влияет.

**Почему ×1,1**
- **Товар 1:** нехватка единицы обходится примерно в 7 (недополученная прибыль 3 + неустойка 4). При ×1,2 излишек около 7 единиц в день копится и через 8 дней списывается. Это примерно 35 в день на списании плюс около 20 на хранении — заметно больше, чем стоит небольшая нехватка при запасе ×1,05–1,1. Поэтому ×1,2 (кандидат 0) слишком много.
- **Товар 1, обратная сторона:** ×1,0 (кандидаты 3, 7 и вторая половина 5) в среднем ниже спроса, и нехватка регулярна.
- **Товар 0:** нехватка единицы стоит около 17 (9 + 8), списание — около 10. Небольшой запас выгоден. Но при ×1,2 излишек примерно 5–6 единиц в день сгорает через 5 дней. Коэффициент ×1,1 даёт запас против колебаний (около ±11 единиц в день) и не накапливает большие списания.

Кандидат 4 держит умеренный запас по обоим товарам и не попадает ни в одну крайность, поэтому у него наибольший ожидаемый итог.

I pick **Candidate 4**. This is an estimate worked out in my head with no simulation, so the gaps between the top plans are approximate.

**Validity.** Candidate 1 has only 28 order pairs, and the task requires exactly 30, so I dropped it.

**How I compared the plans.** An order placed on day t arrives on day t+2, so each order is matched against the forecast for day t+2. Each plan is roughly the forecast times a fixed multiplier:

| Candidate | Product 0 | Product 1 | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 1.00 | 1.00 | Exactly the forecast |
| 6 | ≈1.05 | ≈1.05 | |
| 4 | ≈1.10 | ≈1.09 | |
| 7 | ≈1.20 | 1.00 | |
| 0 | ≈1.25 | ≈1.25 | |
| 5 | ≈1.15, then 1.00 | ≈1.15, then 1.00 | Higher multiplier only for the first half |
| 2 | ≈1.07 | ≈1.07 | Orders every other day, two days' demand at once |

**Short vs. over for each unit.**
- **Product 0:** one unit short loses the margin of 9 plus a penalty of 8, so 17. One unit extra mostly costs holding of 0.6 a day. It is only lost (cost 10) if it spoils after 5 days. The break-even level is about 17 / (17 + 10) ≈ 0.63, which argues for ordering about 10–15% above the forecast.
- **Product 1:** one unit short costs 3 + 4 = 7. One unit extra costs at most 5 if it spoils, and shelf life is 8 days. The break-even level is about 0.58, so a smaller cushion of about 5–10% fits.
- The average demand multiplier is about 1.046, so ordering exactly the forecast (Candidate 3) is already short on average.

**Why the others lose:**
- **Candidates 3 and 6** are at or just above average demand. With 30 days of random demand they run short fairly often, and shortages are the expensive side.
- **Candidate 0** orders 25% extra on both products. That surplus builds up, spoils, and gets thrown away while also paying for holding. For product 1 in particular, that waste costs more than the shortages it prevents.
- **Candidate 7** has a reasonable cushion for product 0 but none for product 1, so it runs short there.
- **Candidate 5** drops its cushion in the second half and loses the protection it had early on.
- **Candidate 2** saves 14 days of fixed fees (14 × 30 = 420). But holding the second day's stock overnight costs about 21.6 for product 0 plus 18 for product 1, so ≈39.6 per two-day cycle. That's slightly more than the 30 it saves each cycle, so overall it comes out about even or a little worse than ordering daily.

**Robustness.** Candidate 4's cushions (≈1.10 for product 0, ≈1.09 for product 1) fit both of these targets best. That also makes it the most stable choice when actual demand lands well above or below the forecast.

The first two days will be short whatever the plan, because the first orders only arrive on day 2.

I'd pick **Candidate 4**, but with only moderate confidence. Everything below is a rough hand estimate, not a simulation.

**Disqualified.** Candidate 1 lists only 28 order pairs, and the rules require exactly 30.

**Common to all plans.** An order placed on day t arrives on day t+2 and covers demand on that day. Starting stock (50 and 46) cannot cover days 0–1 (demand 71 and 67), so every plan takes the same shortage there.

**How the plans differ.** Each is mostly the forecast scaled by some factor (the forecast is mu, two days ahead):
- Candidate 3: exactly the forecast (factor 1.0).
- Candidate 6: about 1.05.
- Candidate 4: about 1.10 for both products.
- Candidate 7: about 1.2 for product 0 and 1.0 for product 1.
- Candidate 0: about 1.25 for both.
- Candidate 5: about 1.2 for the first two weeks, then 1.0.
- Candidate 2: orders every other day, about 1.07 times two days' demand.

**The trade-off.** Unsold stock carries over to later days. So over the whole horizon, shortage minus waste roughly equals (1.046 − factor) × total demand, where 1.046 is the average demand multiplier.
- For product 0, a missed sale costs 17 (lost margin 9 plus penalty 8), and a wasted unit costs 10.
- For product 1, those are 7 and 5.
- Ordering at 1.0–1.046 leaves a shortfall that grows like a reflected random walk, roughly 50–80 units of product 0 over the horizon. That costs more than the extra waste at factor 1.1.
- At 1.2–1.25, product 0 wastes about 150–200 extra units (≈10 each) plus storage. That costs more than the shortages it prevents.
- My rough estimate puts the best factor near 1.1 for both products, which is Candidate 4.

**Candidate 2.** Ordering every other day saves 13 order fees (390). But half of each delivery sits in stock an extra night, about 40 in storage per pair of days, or about 560 in total. That makes it slightly worse than a similar daily plan.

**Robustness.** A modest buffer of about 10% over the forecast absorbs demand swings of ±30% better than ordering exactly the forecast. It also avoids the guaranteed waste of a 20–25% buffer.

I pick **Candidate 4**. This comes from rough mental estimates, not an exact calculation.

**What every plan shares.** Every order arrives two days later. The starting stock is 50 units of product 0 against 71 units of demand on days 0–1, so a shortage of about 21 units happens whatever the plan.

**Unsold stock carries over cheaply.** With FIFO selling and shelf lives of 5 and 8 days, surplus stock rarely spoils. It just carries over at 0.6 or 0.4 per unit per day. The real cost of over-ordering shows up at the end, when leftover stock is worth nothing. Running short costs more:
- **Product 0:** a lost unit costs 9 of lost margin plus an 8 penalty, so 17. A unit ordered but never sold costs 10.
- **Product 1:** a lost unit costs 3 plus 4, so 7. An unsold unit costs 5.

Ordering slightly above average demand pays off.

**Candidates by order size:**
- **Candidate 3** orders exactly the forecast. Actual demand averages about 1.046 × forecast, so it runs short often. Worst of the reasonable options.
- **Candidate 6** orders about 1.05 × forecast, which is almost exactly average demand. Stock does a random walk with no upward drift, and shortages stay frequent.
- **Candidate 4** orders about 1.10 × forecast. The small surplus builds a buffer of about one standard deviation within a few days without spoiling. The waste at the end is about 50 units of product 0 and 70 of product 1. Shortages eat some of that surplus along the way, so the real leftover is smaller. This is the best balance.
- **Candidate 0** orders about 1.25 × forecast. Surplus builds up to roughly 200 units of product 0 and 250 of product 1. It starts spoiling and ends up wasted, costing about 3,000.
- **Candidate 7** orders about 1.2 × forecast for product 0, which is too much, and only the forecast for product 1, which is too little.
- **Candidate 5** orders about 1.15 × forecast in the first half and only the forecast in the second, so it under-orders late.
- **Candidate 2** orders every other day at about 1.07 × the two-day forecast. That saves about 30 in order fees per two days. But each delivery has to hold the next day's demand overnight, which costs about 0.6×36 + 0.4×45 ≈ 40 per two days. The net is a small loss compared with a similar daily plan.
- **Candidate 1** has only 28 pairs instead of the required 30, so the plan is probably invalid. Its order sizes otherwise sit close to Candidate 4's.

**Выбор: кандидат 4.** Уверенность умеренная: главный соперник — кандидат 2, и разница между ними небольшая. Всё посчитано в уме по прогнозным значениям, без точной пошаговой симуляции.

- **Кандидат 1 нарушает условие.** В его плане 28 пар вместо требуемых ровно 30.
- **Как устроены остальные планы.** Заказ дня t приходит в день t+2. Почти все кандидаты заказывают прогноз спроса на день t+2, умноженный на постоянный коэффициент.
  - Кандидат 3 заказывает ровно прогноз (×1,0).
  - Кандидат 6 — примерно ×1,04.
  - Кандидат 4 — примерно ×1,10.
  - Кандидат 0 — примерно ×1,25.
  - Кандидат 7 — примерно ×1,2 по товару 0 и ×1,0 по товару 1.
  - Кандидат 5 — примерно ×1,15 в первой половине и ×1,0 во второй.
- **Средний спрос выше прогноза.** Средний множитель ≈ 1,046, поэтому заказ «ровно по прогнозу» в среднем систематически отстаёт от спроса. Нехватка стоит дорого: по товару 0 это упущенная маржа 9 плюс неустойка 8, всего 17 за единицу; по товару 1 — 3 + 4 = 7. Излишек же не пропадает сразу. Он переходит на следующий день, и с ним по товару 0 теряется в основном только хранение 0,6 в день. Отсюда умеренный перезаказ выгоден, и кандидаты 3 и 6 проигрывают на неустойках.
- **Перезаказ ×1,25 — слишком много.** У кандидата 0 излишек по товару 0 копится примерно по 7 единиц в день. Он растёт в дорогое хранение, а затем списывается по сроку годности, около 70 в день. У кандидата 7 та же проблема по товару 0.
- **Кандидат 4 (×1,10) держит баланс.** Запас прирастает примерно на 2 единицы в день. Этого хватает как страховки от колебаний спроса, а хранение и списания остаются небольшими.
- **Кандидат 2 — почти на равных.** Он заказывает раз в два дня примерно ×1,07. Так он экономит около 420 на ежедневной плате 30. Но примерно столько же уходит на хранение лишнего дня запаса, около 39 за каждую пару дней. Кроме того, крупные партии (например, 70 + 136 единиц в день 22) вместе с остатками подходят к лимиту склада 256, и излишек при приходе может пропасть.

**Choice: candidate 4 — moderate confidence.** I did the math in my head with rough estimates, not a step-by-step run of every day. The only firm result is that candidate 1 is invalid.

1. **Candidate 1 is out.** Its plan has 28 pairs, and the rules require exactly 30.

2. **What each plan does.** An order placed on day t arrives on day t+2, so it is meant to cover the forecast for day t+2. Compared with that forecast, the plans order roughly:

   | Candidate | Product 0 | Product 1 |
   |---|---|---|
   | 3 | 1.0× | 1.0× |
   | 6 | 1.05× | 1.05× |
   | 4 | 1.1× | 1.1× |
   | 7 | 1.2× | 1.0× |
   | 0 | 1.25× | 1.25× |
   | 5 | 1.15× for the first 14 days, then 1.0× | same as product 0 |

   Average demand runs about 1.046× forecast, so any plan at 1.0× is short on average from the start.

3. **Shortages on days 0–1 hit every plan equally.** Starting stock is 50 and 46, against forecast demand of 71 and 67 for those two days.

4. **Cost of ordering too little versus too much:**
   - **Product 0:** a missed sale loses 9 of margin plus a penalty of 8, so 17 per unit. A unit that spoils costs about 10 plus storage. Leftovers can carry over for up to 5 days, so ordering about 1.1–1.2× is justified.
   - **Product 1:** a missed sale costs 3 + 4 = 7. A spoiled unit costs about 5 plus storage. That points to about 1.05–1.1×.
   - **Candidate 0** over-orders by about 7–9 units a day per product, most of which spoils. Spoilage looks like it costs much more than the shortages it prevents.
   - **Candidates 3 and 7** run product 1 below average demand, so they keep paying shortage penalties.
   - **Candidate 5** switches to 1.0× in the second half and gets the same problem.

5. **Candidate 2 (orders every other day) roughly breaks even.** It saves 14 × 30 = 420 in daily order fees. But keeping an extra day's stock overnight costs about 40 per two-day cycle in storage. The day-20 order (72 + 136 units) may also come close to the 256-unit warehouse limit.

6. **Robustness.** Candidate 4 orders a bit more than average demand for both products. That buffer covers day-to-day swings in demand without building up a lot of stock that spoils.

Candidate 7 is the main alternative to 4: it would only win if extra product 0 is worth more than what it loses by being short on product 1.

**Choice: candidate 3.** I estimated this in my head with a rough model, not a simulation, so treat the cost figures as approximate.

**Disqualified:**
- **Candidate 1** has only 28 pairs, but the rules require exactly 30. I counted it as invalid.

**How the plans compare:**
- **Candidate 3** orders each day exactly the forecast for the day the order arrives (day t+2). Average demand runs about 4.6 % above forecast (multiplier mean ≈ 1.046), so supply falls slightly short.
- **Candidates 6, 4, 7 and 0** scale those quantities up by about ×1.05, ×1.1, ×1.2 (product 0 only in candidate 7) and ×1.25.
- **Candidate 5** orders about ×1.15 in the first half of the month, then exactly the forecast.
- **Candidate 2** orders every other day for two days at a time, about ×1.07. That saves about 450 in daily order fees.

**Is extra stock worth it?**
- Day 0 and day 1 run short for every plan, because the starting stock can't cover them.
- From day 2 on, leftover stock is a buffer that drifts with random demand. Each extra buffer unit is held for many days.
- **Product 1:** a buffer unit kept from about day 2 costs about 0.4 × 26 days ≈ 10 in storage, plus 5 if it's never sold. A shortage costs only 7 (lost margin 3 + penalty 4). Extra stock clearly doesn't pay.
- **Product 0:** a buffer unit costs about 0.6 × 26 ≈ 15.6 in storage, plus 10 if it's never sold. A shortage costs 17. It roughly breaks even and becomes a loss once leftovers are counted.
- **So:** under these rules, the smaller the extra stock, the better.

**Rough losses (shortages + leftovers at the end + storage):**

| Candidate | Product 0 | Product 1 | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | ≈ 1770 | ≈ 885 | ≈ 2650 |
| 5 | ≈ 1760 | ≈ 1200 | ≈ 2950 |
| 6 | ≈ 1800 | ≈ 1220 | ≈ 3000 |
| 4 | — | — | ≈ 3800 |
| 7, 0 | — | — | much worse: large buffers, storage and leftovers at the end |

**Candidate 2:** the two-day batches cost about 530 in extra overnight storage, which outweighs the ≈450 saved on order fees. Its supply is also above the forecast. And on day 22, 208 units arrive on top of the existing stock, which can come close to the 256-unit limit.

**Uncertainty:** candidate 3 also stays the best option when demand varies, because its stock rarely builds up. The gap to candidate 5 (≈300) is bigger than the error I'd expect from this estimate, but not by a lot.

Я выбираю **кандидата 5**, но это обоснованная оценка, а не уверенный результат. Я считал в уме и грубо, а кандидаты 4, 5 и 6 оказались близки друг к другу, в пределах нескольких сотен.

**Как я сравнивал.** Заказ дня t приходит в день t+2. Поэтому каждый план — это прогноз спроса на день t+2, умноженный на коэффициент. Средний фактический спрос примерно в 1,046 раза выше прогноза. Если коэффициент выше 1,046, на складе копится запас, который гасит случайные провалы. Если ниже — склад постепенно пустеет, и копятся неустойки.

**Общий для всех убыток.** В день 1 ничего не приходит. Стартового запаса не хватает, и недостача составит около 21 единицы по каждому товару в любом плане. На выбор это не влияет.

**Почему остальные хуже:**
- **Кандидат 1** содержит 28 пар вместо 30 — план не по формату.
- **Кандидат 3** (коэффициент 1,0) заказывает меньше среднего спроса. Запас всё время снижается, по товару 0 теряется примерно 75 единиц продаж. Каждая стоит около 27 (19 выручки плюс 8 неустойки).
- **Кандидат 7** заказывает товар 1 тоже на уровне 1,0, поэтому ему регулярно не хватает товара 1.
- **Кандидат 0** (около 1,25) закупает лишние ~150 единиц товара 0, это около 1500 потерь на закупке. Неустойки он сокращает только примерно на 400.
- **Кандидат 2** заказывает раз в два дня и экономит около 390 на ежедневной плате 30. Но около 550 он теряет на хранении, потому что половина запаса лежит лишнюю ночь. В итоге примерно −160 против похожего ежедневного плана.

**Три самых близких:**

| Кандидат | Коэффициент | Плюсы | Минусы |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6 | ~1,04 весь срок | Наименьшие закупки и хранение | Нет постоянного запаса, около 46 единиц товара 0 недопродано |
| 4 | ~1,10 весь срок | Меньше недопродаж | К концу остаётся много товара, который ничего не стоит (около 700 по товару 0 и 400 по товару 1) |
| 5 | ~1,13 / 1,08 до дня 13, затем 1,0 | Копит запас в начале и расходует его к концу | Больше риск нехватки в последние дни |

Кандидат 5 обходится примерно на 225 дороже кандидата 6 по закупкам. Зато он недопродаёт примерно на 20 единиц меньше, это около 570. По сравнению с кандидатом 4 он оставляет к концу примерно на 475 меньше непроданного товара. Главный риск — недостача в конце срока, если в последние две недели спрос окажется выше прогноза.
